    • 





















    

  • Ranking vs. its contract:
    • 



The format holds: all five entries cite a market cap and P/E value (e.g. GOOGL $3,429.90B and 14.57) plus a named initiative (Project Astra, Azure AI Foundry Labs, G-Assist, Amazon Bedrock, Guardium AI Security), and the output ends with a “Caveat:” line. The line a reviewer would flag is NVDA’s: “The G-Assist project... aligns with its strategy.” G-Assist isn’t one of your gold tokens, so confirm it appears in the NVDA bullets of digest_block and wasn’t pulled from the model’s outside knowledge. The same check applies to “Azure AI Foundry Labs.” The IBM entry is also weak, since its last-place rank leans on a missing-evidence argument (“the lack of disclosed fin...”) rather than a metric, and the Caveat names only IBM even though your retrieval diagnostic showed gaps for Google, NVIDIA and Amazon too. The 80% groundedness (4/5) fits this: claims are mostly supported, with a few that deserve a check. Print ranking_groundedness_raw to see which claims the judge named.


    

  • Routing verdict:
    • 



The run produced FLAGGED at 66.0. Gold accuracy is the component pulling it down: 50% earns only 20 of its 40 points, while the judge mean (73%) and ranking groundedness (80%) each contribute about 22 and 24 of their 30. That 50% is capped by retrieval, not the prompt, because GEPA returned the v1.0 prompt unchanged and only 5 of the 8 held-out rows had the expected token in the context. The change that would move confidence most is fixing retrieval (larger k, different chunk size or overlap, a better embedding model, or query rewriting for acronyms like TPU and NIM). Raising held-out accuracy to 5/8 alone would add 7.5 points, enough to push the score to about 73.5. Supporting multi-company questions like Q3 would lift the judge mean as well.


    

  • Why “a human should look at this” is deployable early:
    • 



A system doesn’t need to be right every time, it needs to know which outputs to trust. The FLAGGED route sends this ranking to an analyst with a specific instruction (verify the weakest-evidence companies first), so an unsupported initiative like G-Assist gets caught before it reaches a client. It is the “I don’t know.” guardrail applied one level up: an honest flag costs less than a confident error. It also gives a measurable improvement path, because each retrieval fix raises the score and shrinks the share of outputs needing review. The caveat is that the score is only as trustworthy as its signals. With 8 held-out rows and judges that penalize correct refusals, validate the thresholds against human review before anyone relies on them.






















🔟 Step 7 — Summary & Future Scope¶
📝 A. Summary / Your Observations about this Project (1 mark)¶
    

  • Retrieval, not the prompt, was the binding constraint. The retrieval diagnostic showed the expected token reached the context for only 15 of 20 gold rows (75%), and the filter made no difference (75% with and without it) because the questions already named the company or a company-specific product. The v1.0 baseline of 10/20 split evenly into 5 retrieval failures (TPU, Quantum, NIM, Flamingo, Trainium), where “I don’t know.” was the correct output, and 5 generation failures. This framing also explained the ceiling for Step 5: prompt optimization could only ever win back the generation half.
    

    • 

  • The out-of-scope probes exposed what each metric actually measures. Q4 (Microsoft’s FY2025 AI revenue) returned exactly “I don’t know.”, which was the right behavior, yet all three judges scored it 1/1/1. Groundedness gave no credit to an honest refusal, and Q3 (a two-company comparison the single-company filter can’t serve) got the same scores for a different reason. The judges can’t separate a correct refusal from a failure. That is why Step 5 optimized against a deterministic substring metric with a word-limit guard and not against judge scores, and why Q4 was excluded from the judge mean.
    

    • 

  • GEPA returned the seed prompt unchanged, so the 3/8 to 4/8 held-out gain cannot be credited to optimization. The v2.0 instructions were word-for-word identical to v1.0 with 0 demos, which points to run-to-run variance or a DSPy-vs-LangChain pipeline difference. The held-out design is what exposed this, since a training-set score would have looked like progress. The prompt was already near its ceiling (4 of the 5 winnable held-out rows), so the honest conclusion is that retrieval quality limits this pipeline.
    

    • 

  • The confidence layer turned a 50%-accurate pipeline into a usable workflow. The run scored 66.0/100 and was routed to FLAGGED, with gold accuracy (50%, worth 20 of its 40 points) as the dragging signal. The final ranking followed its contract (a market cap and P/E value plus a named initiative for every rank), but a reviewer should verify names like G-Assist against the evidence digest, and the Caveat named only IBM despite retrieval gaps elsewhere. Routing borderline outputs to an analyst is the “I don’t know.” principle applied one level up.
    

    • 



🔭 B. Future Scope (1 mark)¶
    

  1. Fix retrieval before anything else. Tune k, chunk size and overlap, try a stronger embedding model, add hybrid keyword (BM25) plus vector search, and rewrite queries for acronym-heavy terms like TPU and NIM. This raises the ceiling on the gold signal, the judge mean and the ranking evidence, and it targets the 5 failures no prompt could fix.
    

    2. 

  2. Multi-company and comparison retrieval. Decompose questions like Q3 into one filtered retrieval per company, then synthesize across them. A single company filter can’t serve cross-company questions, and these are the questions an investment-ranking use case asks most.
    

    3. 

  3. Harden the evaluation. Grow the gold set well beyond 20 rows, with several expected tokens per question and run-to-run repeats, so a one-question change is no longer within noise. Fix the groundedness rubric so a correct refusal is scored as faithful, and calibrate the routing thresholds against human analyst review.
    

    4. 

  4. Data freshness and coverage. Ingest new filings on a schedule with a filing_date metadata field, and expand beyond five companies by sector. This keeps rankings current and tests whether the metadata-filter design scales when look-alike chunks compete for top-k slots.
    

    5. 

  5. Monitoring and a human feedback loop. Log confidence scores, refusal rates and analyst corrections on flagged outputs in production, and feed the corrections back as new gold examples. Rerun GEPA when the training set contains real generation failures, with a larger budget, so the optimizer has headroom to learn from.
    

    6. 

  6. Richer decision logic. Replace the market cap and P/E pair with a wider metric set (growth, margins, AI capex) and per-rank confidence, and add a multi-agent split of retriever, analyst and verifier agents. A verifier that checks every named initiative against the digest would catch unsupported claims automatically, before a human sees them.
    

    7.

    • 

  • A three-metric judge harness cross-validated by an objective gold dataset
    • 

  • A prompt that optimized itself with GEPA — and proved it on held-out questions
